_about: The plain-language headline findings on the Highlights page. The page prints only what is here and in report.generated.json: every number in a sentence is a {{placeholder}} filled from `figures` below, or from REPORT.appeals / REPORT.supremeDelay where the key is marked `generated`. To correct a figure, change it here (or regenerate report.generated.json); never edit a number into the text. `source` names the research card that holds the denominator, unit, snapshot date and script. Figures checked by the Day 5 independent recomputation (work/2026-11-01-research/verify/VERIFY.md), 2026-11-07.
status: Draft for review, not published. Figures checked by an independent recomputation on 7 November 2026; the court-judgment readings are an agent's reading, not a legal review.

findings.headline: Most complaints are closed before a full investigation, and no reason is given
findings.explain: In {{fy}} the CIAA closed {{shelved}} complaints ({{shelvedPct}} of those it dealt with) without a full investigation, and sent only {{toInv}} ({{toInvPct}}) on for a full investigation. Its reports give no reason for any closure, so nobody outside the CIAA can tell why.

findings.headline: After a full investigation, the CIAA now shelves most cases instead of charging them
findings.explain: In {{fyThen}} it took {{filedThen}} investigated cases to court and shelved {{shelvedThenPct}} of its decisions. By {{fyNow}} it took {{filedNow}} to court and shelved {{shelvedNowPct}}. The change came within two years and has not reversed. No case-by-case reason is published for these closures.

findings.headline: Thousands of complaints wait, and nobody says for how long
findings.explain: At the end of {{fy}}, {{carried}} complaints (about {{share}} of those on the books) were carried into the next year. The CIAA's report for that year says how many are waiting and promises to clear "old complaints" first, but does not say how long any of them has waited.
findings.source: stages/1-3-SCREENING.md; GAPS 1.3, checked in the 35th report text 2026-11-07

findings.headline: A person who complains cannot follow what happens to the complaint
findings.explain: When we checked the CIAA's website on {{checked}}, and again on {{rechecked}}, it gave no complaint number and no way to look up a complaint's status. A CIAA notice dated 17 Kartik 2083 says its online complaint portal is being upgraded, and asks people to complain by email, phone, post or in person.

findings.headline: About 4 in 10 cases the CIAA takes to court end in full acquittal, after a full investigation
findings.explain: Of {{decided}} CIAA cases the Special Court has decided, {{acq}} ({{acqPct}}) ended with every defendant acquitted. It is getting worse: about {{earlyShare}} verdicts ended this way in {{earlyYears}}, and {{lateShare}} in {{lateYears}} ({{lateNoStingPct}} leaving out {{stingYear}}, when the sting-money ruling cleared most bribery cases). The CIAA's own report gives the same picture ({{ciaaPct}} won in those five years) but counts a partial conviction as a win. Each lost case had already cost a full investigation. Acquitted cases then spent a median {{acqYears}} years in court, against {{convYears}} for full convictions, and their charge sheets claimed at least Rs {{bigo}} in loss or gain (बिगो). How long the CIAA spent investigating them is not published. In the acquittal judgments we read, the court most often said the evidence did not prove the charge or the act charged was not the offence. It never blamed the trial.
findings.caveat: Cases, not people. Verdict years are Nepali fiscal years. The बिगो is a lower bound read from judgment texts.
findings.source: trial-acquittals/FINDING.md (card 6.5); court record 2026-10-08; CIAA 35th annual report, table 3.12

findings.headline: The public cannot see which defendants were convicted and which were cleared
findings.explain: The court's public case page gives one outcome for the whole case. When a case is "partly upheld", it does not say who was convicted. That is only in the full judgment, on a separate page, and some judgments are never uploaded. This affects {{people}} of the {{all}} defendant records (about {{share}}).

findings.headline: When the court acquits, it usually says the charge was not proved, or was not a crime; it sometimes says the CIAA charged selectively
findings.explain: In the {{read}} acquittal judgments we read, the court said the evidence did not prove the charge in {{evid}}, that what was charged was not the offence (no loss, no bad intent or the wrong offence) in {{charge}}, and named a flaw in the CIAA's investigation in {{inv}}. Reading every judgment that mentions it, we found {{selective}} where the court cleared people partly because the CIAA charged some and left out others who did the same, including the wide-body aircraft and Pashupatinath Jalahari cases. The CIAA publishes no review of why it loses.
findings.caveat: Read with AI software, not yet reviewed by a lawyer; 31 judgments is a sample.

findings.headline: Appeals go one way: convictions are often overturned, acquittals almost never
findings.explain: When a convicted person appeals, the Supreme Court fully overturns the conviction in about 4 of 10 trials ({{defRev}} of {{defDec}}). When the government appeals an acquittal, it wins in about 1 of 100 ({{govRev}} of {{govDec}}).
findings.source: headline/FINDINGS.md H1 (per trial, appeal links as of 2026-11-03)

findings.headline: Overturned convictions mostly fail on how the case was investigated and proved
findings.explain: In the {{read}} overturned convictions we read, the Supreme Court pointed to the investigation in {{inv}}, to bribe money the CIAA itself supplied (evidence the Constitutional Bench ruled out in 2021) in {{sting}}, and to the charge in {{charge}}. Of all the trials whose appeal judgment cites that 2021 ruling, {{stingPct}} ended with the conviction overturned.
findings.caveat: Read with AI software, not yet reviewed by a lawyer; 16 judgments is a sample.

findings.headline: About 1 in 5 acquittals never gets a government appeal, and no reason is published
findings.explain: For {{none}} of {{judgeable}} acquittals old enough to judge ({{pct}}), we found no government appeal in any record. The CIAA publishes how often it decides not to appeal, but no reasons and no list of the cases.

findings.headline: An appeal takes about four years, and more than one in four takes over six
findings.explain: Counting the appeals still waiting, half of those registered {{from}}–{{to}} took more than {{km}} years to decide; {{over6}} of the decided ones took over six. A convicted person's appeal waits longer, about {{person}} years.
findings.source: stages/8.2-DURATION.md (origin universe, Supreme Court records collected 2 November 2026)

findings.headline: About 3 in 4 scheduled hearings do not happen, mostly for the court's own reasons
findings.explain: Of {{listings}} times a corruption appeal was put on the Supreme Court's list, {{notPct}} ended without the bench taking it up. In {{courtShare}} of those, the reason was on the court's side: the list was not reached, a judge could not sit on the case, or the bench did not sit. The next date was typically about {{gap}} later.
findings.source: report/07-appeal-decided.md and stages/CARD_8.3.md (appeals numbered 070-CR- onward, court case pages 2–3 Nov 2026; 77.1%, court side 58.2% of listings); median 58 days to the next listing, stages/hearings/gap_after_unproductive.py --070

findings.headline: 730 open appeals have never been listed for a hearing
findings.explain: Of the {{pending}} corruption appeals still open, {{never}} ({{pct}}) have never once been put on a hearing list. They have waited a median of about {{months}} months since they were registered.

findings.headline: After the September 2025 arson, 865 open appeals still have no file, and decisions have fallen by more than half
findings.explain: The Supreme Court was set on fire on 9 September 2025. Fourteen months later, {{lost}} pending corruption appeals are still marked "file destroyed, not recovered", and {{notListedPct}} of them have not been listed since. In the 14 months after the fire the court decided {{after}} of the appeals pending; in the 14 months before, during a drive to clear old cases, {{before}}.

findings.headline: The public cannot follow a case from trial to appeal
findings.explain: No public court record says which Special Court trial an appeal comes from. We rebuilt the links by hand from judgments, the CIAA's register and names; {{unlinked}} of {{all}} appeals still could not be linked to any trial.

findings.headline: No one publishes how much is recovered from corruption judgments
findings.explain: The courts publish one fine ledger for every kind of case, and "disposed of" includes prison served instead of payment. Outside one or two courts, about {{share}} of that ledger is disposed of in a year. No institution publishes the figure for corruption.
findings.source: RESEARCH-INVENTORY entry 10 (11–12%); Supreme Court annual reports 2075/76–2081/82
